what_its_for: Mesalamine is used to treat and prevent flare-ups of ulcerative colitis, a condition that causes inflammation and sores in your large intestine (colon) and rectum. It works by reducing inflammation directly in the lining of your intestine to help relieve symptoms like diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and stomach pain.
how_to_take: Mesalamine comes in several forms: tablets, capsules, rectal suppositories, and rectal enemas. Always take the form your doctor prescribed. Swallow tablets and capsules whole — do not crush, break, or chew them. Take tablets and capsules with a full glass of water. For rectal suppositories, insert them into your rectum and try to hold them in for at least 1 to 3 hours, or as long as possible. For rectal enemas, shake the bottle well, insert the tip into your rectum while lying on your left side, and try to hold the liquid in for at least 8 hours (best used at bedtime). Wash your hands before and after using rectal forms.
dosing: Your dose depends on the form you are taking and the condition being treated. Typical adult doses are: Tablets (Asacol HD): 1.6 g three times daily with meals during a flare; Capsules (Delzicol): 800 mg three times daily; Extended-release tablets (Lialda): 2.4 to 4.8 g once daily with a meal; Capsules (Pentasa): 1 g four times daily; Suppositories (Canasa): 1 g inserted rectally once daily at bedtime; Enemas (Rowasa): 4 g retained overnight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store mesalamine tablets and capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep rectal enema bottles at room temperature and use them within the expiration date once opened. Keep suppositories away from heat and do not refrigerate unless directed. Keep all forms out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids at the same time as mesalamine, as they may affect how the medicine is released in your body — ask your pharmacist about timing. Avoid NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) unless your doctor approves, as they may reduce the effectiveness of mesalamine. Do not use any rectal products (creams, laxatives) in your rectum at the same time without asking your doctor. Tell your doctor if you are taking azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, as mesalamine can increase their side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, or fast heartbeat; severe stomach pain, cramping, or bloody diarrhea that gets worse (this could be a rare reaction called 'mesalamine-induced colitis'); signs of a kidney problem such as less urination, swelling in your legs or feet, or unusual fatigue; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe nausea; severe headache, fever, or rash; or if your symptoms do not improve after a few weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within a few days to a few weeks of starting mesalamine. However, it may take up to 6 weeks to see the full benefit during a flare-up. For maintenance therapy (preventing flare-ups), it is important to keep taking mesalamine even when you feel well. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Kidney or liver problems: Mesalamine is processed by the kidneys, so if you have kidney or liver disease, tell your doctor before starting this medicine — your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you. Pregnancy: Mesalamine is generally considered low risk during pregnancy, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of mesalamine can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits if you are breastfeeding. Children: Some forms of mesalamine are approved for children, but dosing is based on weight. Only give mesalamine to a child if prescribed by their doctor. Elderly patients: Older adults may be at higher risk for kidney problems, so regular monitoring may be needed.
